visual.general_description: A conceptual diagram of oxygen/energy cost, work output and clinical phenotypes.
visual.detailed_description: An unlettered grayscale conceptual diagram has a wide top definition box, a narrow lower-left icon column and a larger lower-right four-quadrant map. Top text defines VO2 as oxygen volume, CO2 as carbon-dioxide production, EE as energy expenditure and W as work output, with MEC=VO2/W and MEF=W/EE. The left column shows a cloud with opposed internal up/down arrows and VO2/VCO2 labels; a black downward arrow points to lung and heart outline icons, followed by a bent-leg outline and an oval with protruding short marks around the EE label. Another black downward arrow points toward the lower W/work-output icon cluster. The right map has a horizontal Mechanical Economy (mL/min/watt) axis pointing right from low to high and a vertical Mechanical Efficiency (%) axis pointing upward from low to high. Thin lines create four quadrants: Optimal Function at upper left, High cost at upper right, Subclinical inefficiency at lower left and Global Inefficiency at lower right, with small profile/check or warning icons. Opposed curved arrows lie at the quadrant intersection. Bottom text says exercise training aims toward the top-left and describes within-subject interpretation and low-workload gross-MEC limitations. There are no patient measurements, numerical axis ticks or microscopy/radiologic acquisitions.

evidence.quote: Treadmill exercise testing is the preferred testing modality in patients with rate response devices []. The patient also reported exercise‐related fatigue and breathlessness out of proportion to the workload, despite optimal medical therapy.

clinical_significance.statement: Authors identify the initial DDDR exercise test in panel A as showing minimal heart-rate-response change with CRT-D working too aggressively.

limitations: These are graphs of exercise measurements, not ECG waveform strips or imaging acquisitions. Phase A/B/C labels are exact pixels; printed summary measurements remain pixel-only until parent clinical review.

evidence.quote: Pre‐to‐post CR, there was a +9% change in VO_(2peak) (1 mL/kg/min, 0.3 MET) and a 61% change in W _(peak) (48 W) (Table 1). These can be explained by the improvements in MEC and MEF as underlying physiological determinants of VO_(2peak) (Figures 1 and 4). These results highlight the role of peripheral adaptations as a significant driver of exercise performance in patients with HFrEF and CRT‐D, which is clinically relevant and consistent with the evidence. By understanding the concepts of MEC and MEF, clinicians can gain a more accurate assessment of an individual's ability to convert metabolic energy into mechanical work, offering a plausible hypothesis for the commonly seen discrepancy between VO_(2peak) and W _(peak) changes. Incorporating MEC and MEF into clinical assessments can guide the development of more targeted interventions in patients with HFrEF with a CRT‐D, and therefore MEC and MEF should be routinely measured and reported for assessing rehabilitation outcomes.

clinical_significance.statement: The authors report pre-to-post rehabilitation exercise-performance improvements in this patient.

limitations: These are graphs of exercise measurements, not ECG waveform strips or imaging acquisitions. Phase A/B/C labels are exact pixels; printed summary measurements remain pixel-only until parent clinical review.

caption_claims.value: Accumulated load of supervised exercise training across cardiac rehabilitation based on the session-RPE method

evidence.quote: Progressive overload is a staple of the training process [, ]. We evaluated all patients' subjective and objective responses to each workload after each rehabilitation day to confirm they were within prescribed ranges []. If needed, the clinical team revised the exercise target heart rate and RPE, and external workloads were adjusted to bring both within prescribed range in the next session. The patient attended 33 outpatient hospital‐based CR exercise sessions with 87% completed as planned. Exercise target heart rate and Session‐RPE targets were met on 94% of sessions. All sessions lasted for the planned duration. Average exercise frequency was 2.6 sessions/week. Exercise training volume quantification was based on the Session‐RPE method [, , ]. Median daily exercise volume was 720 arbitrary units, and total accumulated training volume was 23,280 arbitrary units (Figure 3).

clinical_significance.statement: The authors report 33 attended outpatient sessions, median daily load 720 arbitrary units and total 23,280 arbitrary units using Session-RPE.

limitations: The image contains 38 session positions and “36 Planned”/“38 booked” annotations while prose reports 33 attended sessions. These are retained with distinct labels; no attendance denominator or exact series correction is invented.

evidence.quote: Conceptual framework linking Mechanical Economy (MEC) and Mechanical Efficiency (MEF) to clinical phenotypes and training response in a 57‐year‐old male patient with HFrEF and a CRT‐D. After exercise‐based cardiac rehabilitation peak workload increased disproportionately to modest changes in peak oxygen consuption. MEC/MEF improved at physiological thresholds and peak effort. MEC and MEF reveal disproportionate gains in external work for metabolic cost and should be reported alongside traditional cardiopulmonary outcomes in cardiac rehabilitation.
